motivation_or_abstract: Bandit algorithms are usually analyzed as if their action stream were a private byproduct of learning. In practice the action stream is the most public thing about a deployed system: displayed prices, shown ads, recommended items, and prescribed treatments are all observable, while rewards are not. We ask a simple question: how much does a bandit algorithm reveal to an observer who sees only which arm was pulled at each round? We formalize a passive eavesdropper performing property inference on the action log, with two targets: identifying the optimal arm and estimating the gap vector. First, we show that action logs are startlingly informative. Beyond a naive argmax-of-counts attack, we derive algorithm-aware likelihood attacks that invert the deterministic index dynamics of UCB and successive elimination: the times at which the played arm switches pin down the empirical means, letting an observer estimate gaps at a rate within a constant factor of an observer who saw all the rewards. A sequential Monte Carlo attack extends this to Thompson Sampling and EXP3. Second, we prove this leakage is unavoidable: via a Fano/change-of-measure argument, any algorithm with regret R_T admits an attacker whose best-arm error probability is O(R_T / (Delta T)), so epsilon-secrecy forces linear regret with an explicit constant, yielding a matching regret-secrecy frontier. We then design decoy-set and count-symmetrization wrappers that attain this frontier, and show that DP-bandit algorithms sit far from it. Finally we flip the attack into an algorithm: a second agent that merely watches a UCB agent achieves near-optimal regret with zero exploration cost, making exploration a public good. Experiments on synthetic bandits and real recommendation logs quantify per-algorithm leakage.
problem_statement: The sequence of arms pulled by a bandit algorithm -- with no reward information whatsoever -- is nearly a sufficient statistic for the reward means the algorithm has learned, so any low-regret algorithm necessarily broadcasts its private conclusions to any passive observer; there is a quantifiable Pareto frontier between regret and 'aggregate secrecy' that differential privacy for bandits does not address at all.

motivation_or_abstract: Bandit theory measures the cost of learning in pulls, implicitly assuming each pull reveals a real number for free. In many deployments the expensive resource is not the pull but the *resolution* of the observation: a human annotator can give a thumbs-up cheaply or a fine-grained score expensively, a sensor can report a coarse bin or a calibrated value, and a client can transmit one bit or a float. We introduce the bit-budgeted bandit, in which the learner selects an arm and a quantizer (a set of at most m bits' worth of measurement questions about the realized reward) each round, and is charged for bits rather than rounds. We develop the resulting bit complexity theory. First, we show that classical variance adaptivity is fragile under blind quantization: with any fixed, history-independent quantizer of m bits, the achievable instance-dependent regret scales with max(sigma^2, 4^{-m}) log T / Delta, so attaining full-precision performance requires Theta(log(1/sigma)) bits per pull -- resolution must be matched to the noise level, not to the gap. Second, we show interactivity removes this cost: an adaptive-window dithering scheme (AQ-UCB) that shrinks its measurement range with its own confidence interval attains sigma^2 log T / Delta regret with a single bit per pull for sub-Gaussian rewards, giving a provable interactive/non-interactive separation. Third, we show quantization is an implicit robust mean estimator, so one-bit feedback matches truncated-mean bandits under heavy tails without moment tuning. Simulations validate the predicted scalings, and replay experiments on recommendation data instantiate the theory as a concrete design rule for how many levels a feedback scale should have.
problem_statement: Sample complexity is the wrong currency when observations are expensive to *measure* rather than to *obtain*: we hypothesize that bandit learning has a distinct bit complexity, that a single adaptively placed bit per pull is enough to match full-precision instance-dependent regret up to constants for sub-Gaussian rewards, and that non-interactive (fixed-resolution) feedback provably needs Theta(log(1/sigma)) bits per pull, yielding a concrete design rule -- feedback resolution should match observation noise, not the reward gap.

motivation_or_abstract: Bandit algorithms maximize the mean of a number, but in most applications that number is an arbitrary encoding of an ordinal signal: a five-star rating, a 1-10 LLM-judge score, a clinical severity grade. Mapping stars to utilities as 1,2,3,4,5 rather than 1,2,3,4,10 is a modelling choice that no one validates, and it can flip which arm is best. We formalize the monotone-robust bandit: rewards take values in an ordered set of L levels, the true utility u is an unknown increasing function, and the learner is judged by regret maximized over all utilities consistent with what it knows. First, we characterize identifiability: an arm is optimal for every utility exactly when it first-order stochastically dominates the others, and we show, via non-transitive-dice constructions, that the pairwise majority relation among arm distributions can cycle. Consequently any algorithm that only samples rewards -- however many -- must incur linear worst-case regret if it commits to a single arm, whereas a randomized mixture provably attains a strictly smaller minimax regret given by the value of a zero-sum game between the learner and the utility. We give MR-UCB, which maintains DKW-style CDF confidence bands, solves the induced robust game by a linear program, and plays the maximin mixture; it attains sublinear regret with respect to the game value, with rates governed by a dominance gap rather than a mean gap. Second, we add a second feedback channel: standard-gamble queries about the utility scale. We prove O(L log(1/eps)) queries -- independent of the number of arms and horizon -- suffice for eps-max-regret, give a query lower bound, and a max-regret-reduction query rule. Finally, we audit MovieLens, Amazon reviews, Yelp and public LLM-judge scores, quantifying how often mean-based rankings and leaderboards are scale artifacts.
problem_statement: Almost every deployed bandit optimizes the mean of an arbitrarily chosen numerical encoding of an ordinal signal (1-5 stars, 1-10 judge scores, clinical grades), yet the identity of the best arm is *not* invariant to monotone re-encodings of that signal; we hypothesize (i) such rank reversals and even non-transitive dominance cycles are common in real logged feedback, (ii) no algorithm that only samples rewards can resolve them, so a scale-free learner must play a randomized minimax-regret mixture over arms, and (iii) a handful of cheap utility-elicitation queries (O(L log 1/eps) standard-gamble comparisons over the L observation levels, independent of the number of arms and the horizon) suffices to recover near-optimal single-arm performance.

motivation_or_abstract: In-context learning is almost universally studied with prompts drawn from a single stationary task, and the field has even sought permutation-invariant ICL algorithms. Yet real contexts drift: instructions get revised mid-conversation, user preferences change, tool APIs update, and streaming data shifts. We ask a simple question: what does an LLM do when the labeling rule changes in the middle of its context? We construct a controlled benchmark of drifting prompts (label remappings, in-context linear regression with a changing weight vector, boolean-function switches, output-format and language switches, and preference reversals) in which the first n_pre demonstrations follow rule A and the next n_post follow rule B, and we compare model predictions against two reference learners: an exchangeable Bayesian posterior over rules (which cannot discount stale evidence) and a recency-discounted learner. We find and characterize 'stale-evidence anchoring': post-switch accuracy is governed by the *ratio* n_post/(n_pre+n_post) rather than by absolute recency, so more pre-switch evidence makes adaptation proportionally slower — a distinct scaling law from stationary ICL curves. Mechanistically, we show via task-vector probes and logit lens that the model's internal task representation after a switch is a count-weighted convex blend of the two task encodings, and that a small set of task-encoding heads carries this blend. Finally, we show that a training-free intervention — exponential attention-logit discounting over demonstration blocks in those heads, gated by a linear 'drift detector' probe read off the residual stream — recovers most of the oracle post-switch accuracy while leaving stationary ICL intact. Small-transformer pretraining experiments reveal a stability-plasticity tradeoff: meta-training with drifting contexts yields recency-adaptive ICL at a measurable cost in stationary sample efficiency.
problem_statement: Because ICL behaves like an (approximately) exchangeable Bayesian learner over latent tasks, LLMs cannot discount obsolete demonstrations: when the labeling rule changes in the middle of a context, the cost of adapting scales with the *number* of pre-switch examples rather than their recency, and the model's internal task representation becomes a count-weighted blend of old and new tasks. If this diagnosis is right, then injecting a purely inference-time recency prior into a small set of task-encoding attention heads should restore adaptivity without harming stationary ICL.

motivation_or_abstract: Every study of in-context learning feeds the model positive evidence: examples of what the answer *is*. Human and Bayesian learners also learn from what the answer is *not*. We ask a simple question with a clean experimental handle: can LLMs learn in-context from explicitly negative demonstrations, and if not, why? Our key design is information matching. In a binary task, 'x is NOT negative' is logically identical to 'x is positive', so a negative demonstration carries exactly the same bits as a positive one; in a k-way task, a negative demonstration carries a precisely computable log(k/(k-1)) bits. This lets us define negative-evidence efficiency, the fraction of available eliminative information an LLM converts into accuracy, and to compare directly against a Bayesian oracle. Across open models (Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1, Gemma-2, OLMo-2, 0.5B-70B) and synthetic rule-induction, classification, and constraint-satisfaction tasks, we predict and test a strong asymmetry: negative demonstrations yield a small fraction of the gain of information-equivalent positive ones, and often *raise* the probability of the very label they exclude — negation-as-association. Mechanistically, we attribute this to label-copying induction heads that attend to the demonstration answer token while remaining largely insensitive to the polarity marker, showing via per-head logit attribution, polarity probes, and causal patching where polarity information exists but fails to be routed into suppression. We then repair the deficit training-free: (i) verbalized elimination that rewrites negative demos into positive ones, and (ii) polarity-gated inversion of copy-head contributions, recovering most of the oracle gap. Finally, small-transformer meta-training shows eliminative ICL emerges only when pretraining data contains negative evidence, and coincides with the birth of anti-induction heads. As an application, we show that keeping past wrong answers in an agent's context increases repetition of those exact errors, and that our fix reduces it.
problem_statement: In-context learning is driven by positive label copying (induction/copy heads), so LLMs extract far less information from *negative* (eliminative) demonstrations than from information-equivalent positive ones — and in the limit they treat 'x is NOT y' as evidence *for* y. We test this with an exactly information-matched positive-vs-negative demonstration design (in binary tasks a negative demo is logically identical to a positive one), quantify the shortfall in bits relative to a Bayesian oracle, localize it to copy-suppression-deficient heads, and repair it training-free.

motivation_or_abstract: Given the examples {16, 8, 2, 64}, humans confidently infer 'powers of two' rather than 'even numbers', because a random sample of even numbers would be a suspicious coincidence. This inference requires a specific likelihood - the size principle, p(x|h) proportional to 1/|h| - which follows from assuming examples were drawn from *within* the concept (strong or pedagogical sampling). Every Bayesian account of in-context learning posits a posterior over latent tasks, yet none has asked which sampling assumption LLMs encode. We answer this with a simple, quantitative probe: we present LLMs with nested-hypothesis concept-learning prompts (numbers, taxonomic categories, regexes/string patterns, and label-scope classification) in which the examples are consistent with both a narrow and a broad hypothesis, vary the number of consistent examples n from 1 to 8, and measure the generalization gradient over probe items that discriminate the hypotheses. Fitting a one-parameter Bayesian family with likelihood 1/|h|^alpha to model behavior yields an interpretable 'sampling exponent'. Our central prediction is that LLMs sit near alpha = 0 (weak sampling): breadth is driven by surface similarity to the examples, not by the improbability of the coincidence, so redundant consistent examples buy almost no narrowing - unlike humans, who track alpha near 1. We further test whether alpha is a controllable knob by stating the sampling frame explicitly ('a teacher chose these to be maximally informative' vs 'these were randomly encountered'), which changes the normative answer while holding examples fixed. We then explain the deficit: small transformers meta-trained on positive-only strongly-sampled concepts do acquire alpha near 1, whereas incidental/weakly-sampled meta-training yields alpha near 0, indicating a data-distributional rather than architectural origin. Finally, we show a cheap repair (hypothesis-enumeration-with-size CoT) that recovers most human-like narrowing and reduces overgeneralization in a practical rule-induction task, and we show that similarity-based demonstration retrieval systematically produces prompts whose pedagogical information LLMs cannot exploit.
problem_statement: Bayesian accounts of ICL specify a posterior over latent tasks but never test the *likelihood* that generates demonstrations. We hypothesize that LLMs implicitly assume demonstrations are weakly sampled (randomly observed) rather than strongly/pedagogically sampled (deliberately chosen from within the target concept), so they do not obey the size principle: their generalization breadth barely narrows as more mutually-consistent examples arrive, whereas humans and strong-sampling Bayes narrow exponentially. We can measure this as a single interpretable exponent alpha in p(x|h) ~ 1/|h|^alpha estimated from model behavior, show alpha ~ 0 for LLMs, show alpha is largely insensitive to explicit statements about how examples were chosen, and show alpha ~ 1 emerges in small transformers only when meta-training data are actually strongly sampled.

motivation_or_abstract: In-context learning is universally evaluated on deterministic tasks: there is one correct label per input. But most real prediction problems are stochastic, and a competent learner should infer not just the mapping but its noise level. We ask whether LLMs can learn a distribution in context. We build prompts whose demonstrations are drawn from an explicitly noisy rule, P(y=A|x)=p with p known to the experimenter, and compare the model's next-token distribution over label verbalizers with the exact Bayesian posterior predictive. This design yields two interpretable numbers per model: an aleatoric transmission coefficient beta, the slope of model log-odds on true in-context log-odds, and an epistemic sensitivity epsilon, how much predictive entropy shrinks as demonstrations accumulate under a deterministic rule. We predict and test noise blindness: beta far below 1 (predictive distributions collapse toward the majority label, ignoring in-context stochasticity) together with small epsilon (confidence barely tracks evidence quantity), so LLMs' predictive uncertainty is largely decoupled from both components of the ground truth. We further dissociate homoscedastic from heteroscedastic (input-dependent) noise, showing the latter is essentially unlearned. Mechanistically, we train linear probes showing the in-context noise rate *is* linearly decodable from mid-layer activations, i.e. the information is present but not routed to the output; steering along this decoded direction, or an affine logit recalibration conditioned on the decoded rate, recovers most of the gap to the Bayesian oracle at negligible cost. Small transformers meta-trained on stochastic tasks achieve beta near 1, showing the deficit is distributional, not architectural. Finally, on ChaosNLI and other multi-annotator datasets our repair improves prediction of human label distributions over standard few-shot prompting.
problem_statement: Every ICL benchmark assumes a deterministic latent function from x to y, so we do not know whether LLMs can infer a *stochastic* rule in context. We hypothesize an asymmetry we call noise blindness: when demonstrations are generated by a known noisy rule (P(y=A|x)=p), LLMs' predictive distributions transmit only a small fraction of the in-context aleatoric rate (log-odds slope beta << 1, i.e. mode collapse toward the majority label), while simultaneously being nearly insensitive to the epistemic uncertainty that should shrink with the number of demonstrations. Because the noise rate is nonetheless linearly decodable from the residual stream, this is a routing failure that a single training-free steering/recalibration knob can largely repair.

motivation_or_abstract: Parallel test-time compute -- sampling many chains of thought and aggregating by voting or a verifier -- reliably improves accuracy, but the gains saturate quickly and unpredictably. We argue the controlling variable is not the number of samples N but how correlated their errors are. Treating each sample's error as a Bernoulli variable with marginal error rate 1-p and pairwise correlation rho, standard concentration gives an effective sample size N_eff = N/(1+(N-1)rho), predicting that majority-vote accuracy plateaus at a rho-determined ceiling regardless of budget. We first measure (p, rho) per problem for several open models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Math-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) on GSM8K, MATH-500, AMC/AIME, and GPQA-Diamond, and show that a two-parameter N_eff law forecasts measured maj@N and weighted best-of-N curves and their saturation points with low calibration error. Second, we test the hypothesis that RL/long-CoT reasoning training increases rho: at matched pass@1, reasoning-tuned models exhibit higher error correlation and larger pass@N-minus-maj@N gaps than instruct reference methods, explaining why the models built for test-time compute benefit least from parallel sampling. Third, we show rho is an actionable design target: replacing i.i.d. temperature sampling with a *portfolio* of decorrelating operators -- solution-representation variation (natural-language CoT, program-of-thought, backward substitution check, enumeration), and machine-verified answer-preserving problem rewrites -- lowers rho by a large margin and, at matched token cost, dominates self-consistency, adaptive-consistency, and verifier-reranked best-of-N. A cheap two-pilot-sample router further allocates budget across problems. Error correlation gives test-time compute a predictive, controllable axis.
problem_statement: The returns from parallel test-time compute (self-consistency, best-of-N) are governed almost entirely by the *error correlation* between samples, not by their number: an effective-sample-size law acc(N; p, rho) predicts where scaling saturates, and reasoning-optimized (RLVR/long-CoT) models have systematically higher rho than their base/instruct counterparts, so they waste parallel compute. Spending a fixed token budget across low-correlation *solution strategies* (representation and answer-preserving problem-space variation) rather than i.i.d. temperature samples should therefore shift the entire compute-accuracy frontier.

motivation_or_abstract: Offline reinforcement learning datasets are usually collected by a process that was itself improving: replay buffers of an RL run, successive versions of a deployed recommender, or a sequence of increasingly skilled human operators. Standard offline RL discards this structure, pooling all transitions and then constraining the learned policy to stay near the resulting behavior mixture. We argue this throws away the single most useful signal in the log: the direction in which the data-generating policy was already moving. We introduce Chronological Policy Extrapolation (CPX), which (i) partitions a dataset by collection index (or, when timestamps are unavailable, by a return-based pseudo-time), (ii) fits a progress-conditioned policy whose dependence on the progress variable is linear in parameter or feature space --- either via a hypernetwork/linear-embedding conditioning or via simple weight arithmetic between policies trained on early and late data --- and (iii) extrapolates beyond the last observed progress value, theta = theta_late + alpha (theta_late - theta_early), with alpha chosen entirely offline by maximizing a pessimistic (ensemble-lower-bound) critic score on dataset states. CPX is a wrapper: it applies on top of BC, TD3+BC, IQL, or CQL. On D4RL replay-style and mixed-quality datasets we test three claims: extrapolation exceeds the best policy contained in the data; the gain disappears when progress labels are shuffled, confirming the ordering (not extra capacity) is responsible; and the offline critic ranks alpha well enough to keep regret to an oracle alpha small. We further characterize when extrapolation helps versus catastrophically diverges, giving a practical, essentially free addition to any offline RL pipeline.
problem_statement: Most offline RL datasets are logs of a system that was getting better over time, yet algorithms treat them as an unordered bag of transitions and are therefore fundamentally anchored to the average behavior policy. We hypothesize that the intra-dataset ordering (collection time, or a return-based pseudo-time) defines an improvement direction in policy space, and that extrapolating a short distance along this direction --- in policy parameter/embedding space rather than in a conditioning token --- yields policies that outperform every policy present in the data, with the extrapolation magnitude selectable purely offline using a pessimistic critic.

motivation_or_abstract: Conformal prediction promises distribution-free coverage, provided calibration labels are drawn independently of the prediction sets. In deployment this assumption is routinely broken: prediction sets are displayed to the humans or LLM annotators whose answers are later recycled as calibration labels. We show that this creates a performative feedback loop in which coverage becomes self-fulfilling. We model an anchored annotator whose reported label falls inside the displayed set with a probability that increases as the set shrinks, and analyze the resulting recursion on the conformal quantile. We prove that above an anchoring threshold depending only on the anchoring strength and alpha, the recursion has a unique fixed point at which measured coverage equals the nominal 1-alpha while true coverage is strictly and quantifiably lower, and sets contract to (near-)singletons; below the threshold the loop is stable and coverage is retained. We then demonstrate the loop empirically in three settings: (1) simulated anchoring on ImageNet/CIFAR-100 with APS/RAPS scores, (2) anchoring behaviour fit to public human-with-AI labelling datasets, and (3) a fully real closed loop in which an LLM annotator is shown prediction sets on multiple-choice QA and its answers are fed back into recalibration, yielding a 20+ point gap between reported and true coverage within a few rounds. Finally we give two remedies with guarantees: epsilon-blind auditing, where a small randomized fraction of set-withheld labels restores finite-sample validity at a characterized efficiency cost, and level randomization, where jittering the displayed alpha acts as an instrument that identifies the anchoring function and de-biases coverage estimates without any blind labels.
problem_statement: When conformal prediction sets are shown to the annotators (humans or LLMs) whose labels later serve as calibration data, the labels become endogenous to the sets: annotators anchor on displayed candidates, so observed coverage stays at 1-alpha while true coverage collapses and sets shrink toward a degenerate fixed point. We hypothesize (i) this performative loop is provably self-fulfilling above an anchoring threshold, (ii) it occurs empirically with real LLM annotators, and (iii) it can be detected and corrected either by a small fraction of set-blind audit labels or by randomizing the displayed nominal level as an instrument that identifies anchoring strength.

motivation_or_abstract: Conformal prediction is advertised as assumption-light: given exchangeable calibration data, prediction sets attain 1-alpha coverage regardless of the model. We point out a widespread and previously unexamined violation of this premise. Modern predictors — especially LLMs calibrated on public benchmarks — have often already seen part of their calibration data during training. Memorization makes conformity scores on such points anomalously good, in a strictly one-sided way, so the calibrated quantile is too small and the resulting sets under-cover fresh data, while every standard diagnostic (covariate distributions, label quality, split-conformal coverage measured on the same benchmark) looks fine. We formalize leakage as a mixture score shift with a contamination rate rho and a memorization gap g, and derive a tight one-sided lower bound on test coverage that shows how the coverage deficit grows with rho*g and shrinks with calibration-set size; symmetrically, we show that evaluating coverage on a contaminated test split produces a 'coverage illusion' that hides the loss. Empirically, we (i) validate the theory in a controlled setting by fine-tuning small models on a known subset of the calibration pool and sweeping rho; (ii) measure real leakage shift in vision using train/calibration near-duplicates; (iii) measure it in LLMs using verified pretraining-corpus membership via public n-gram indices, and using a temporal-split design with a placebo model whose cutoff postdates both splits, which identifies the memorization component separately from genuine distribution shift. Finally we give three remedies — membership-weighted conformal prediction, membership-group-conditional (Mondrian) calibration, and worst-case alpha inflation — and quantify the efficiency price of restoring validity.
problem_statement: Conformal prediction requires calibration and test points to be exchangeable with respect to the conformity score, but when calibration examples were (partially) seen during pretraining/training, memorization shifts their scores in a strictly favorable, one-sided direction. We hypothesize that this 'leakage shift' causes systematic under-coverage on fresh data that is invisible to standard diagnostics (no covariate shift, no label noise), that its magnitude is predictable from the contamination rate and a measurable memorization gap, and that it can be repaired with membership-weighted or membership-group-conditional calibration at a small efficiency cost.

title: Leaky Calibration: Data Contamination Silently Invalidates Conformal Prediction

motivation_or_abstract: Conformal prediction guarantees coverage only under exchangeability, so its guarantee silently evaporates under distribution shift -- and detecting this requires labeled target data, which is exactly what is unavailable at deployment. We ask a simple question: can coverage be estimated without labels? We observe that replacing the missing target label with the prediction of an *independently trained* second model gives a fully label-free statistic, the pseudo-coverage, i.e. the fraction of target points where model B's prediction lies inside model A's conformal set. Pseudo-coverage is biased by B's error, but we show that its bias is highly structured: across many model pairs it traces a tight linear relationship between in-distribution and out-of-distribution pseudo-coverage whose slope and intercept closely match those of true ID-vs-OOD coverage, a phenomenon we call coverage-on-the-line. We prove that the bias equals a difference of two asymmetric error terms that cancel exactly under a conditional-error-symmetry condition, and that a probit-scaling shift model implies the observed linearity. Empirically, on model zoos over CIFAR-10/100-C, ImageNet-C/R/V2/Sketch, WILDS, and multiple-choice-QA shifts for LLMs, our estimator predicts OOD coverage of APS/RAPS/THR sets to within a few points, far better than nominal, ATC-, confidence-, and importance-weighting-based reference methods. We then close the loop: choosing the source calibration level so that predicted target coverage equals 1-alpha yields target-label-free prediction sets that recover nominal coverage at a modest size cost relative to an oracle calibrated on labeled target data. Finally we map when the method fails -- label shift, spurious-feature shift, and highly correlated model zoos -- and give a label-free diagnostic that flags these cases.
problem_statement: Conformal coverage on shifted data can be estimated, monitored, and restored using only unlabeled target data, because a purely label-free quantity -- the rate at which one model's prediction falls inside another model's conformal set ('pseudo-coverage') -- is strongly linearly related, across model pairs, to the unobservable true coverage; whenever this line is observed to hold, solving for the calibration level that hits nominal predicted coverage yields valid sets under shift with no target labels and no covariate-shift/likelihood-ratio assumptions.

title: Coverage-on-the-Line: Estimating and Restoring Conformal Coverage Under Distribution Shift Without Any Target Labels

motivation_or_abstract: Conformal prediction is celebrated as model-agnostic, and this is often misread as model-invariant: in practice calibration is performed once, with an expensive full-precision checkpoint, while the model actually serving requests is quantized, pruned, distilled, compiled, or executed on a different backend or batch size. We show that this seemingly innocuous mismatch is a distinct source of guarantee failure, model shift, which existing remedies for distribution shift cannot address because there is neither a covariate likelihood ratio nor target labels to adapt to. Empirically, INT4/INT8 post-training quantization and moderate pruning of ImageNet classifiers and open LLMs leave top-1 accuracy nearly intact yet perturb conformity scores enough to push coverage of APS/RAPS/THR sets below nominal, with far larger deficits for rare classes and hard subgroups; reverse mismatch wastes efficiency instead. Our key observation is that, unlike data shift, model shift is identifiable without labels: for any unlabeled input, the score change can be computed for every candidate label, so the worst-case per-example perturbation is an observable quantity. We turn this into Coupled Conformal Calibration: using a labeled calibration set scored by the old model plus an unlabeled pool scored by both models, an order-statistic bound on the perturbation quantile yields prediction sets for the served model with finite-sample coverage at least 1-alpha-beta, together with a tighter (heuristic) monotone score-transport variant. We evaluate coverage, set size, label budget, and conditional validity across compression families, and propose 'conformal fidelity', the alpha-inflation a compression requires, as a new deployment metric.
problem_statement: Conformal prediction is model-agnostic but not model-invariant: its guarantee requires the *same* predictor at calibration and at test time, an assumption routinely violated in deployment because the served model is quantized, pruned, distilled, recompiled, or run on a different backend than the one used for calibration. We hypothesize (i) accuracy-preserving compressions can nevertheless cause statistically significant marginal and severe class/group-conditional under-coverage, (ii) unlike data shift, this 'model shift' is *label-free identifiable* because the change in conformity score can be measured for every candidate label on unlabeled data, and (iii) a simple coupling correction using an unlabeled pool restores finite-sample validity for the served model at a small, measurable set-size cost, yielding a new 'conformal fidelity' axis on which to rank compression methods.

title: Calibrate in FP16, Serve in INT4: Model-Shift Breaks Conformal Coverage, and Label-Free Score Coupling Fixes It

motivation_or_abstract: Conformal prediction is usually presented as free: attach it to any model and get 1-alpha coverage. It is not free -- it costs ground-truth labels, the scarcest resource in exactly the high-stakes domains (pathology, radiology, expert QA) where prediction sets are wanted. We revisit calibration as a label-acquisition problem and observe that split conformal prediction is statistically wasteful: it burns labels to learn one scalar threshold, and the vast majority of labeled points contribute an essentially deterministic coverage indicator because the model is confidently right. We propose ACTIVE-CAL, which (1) computes, for every unlabeled pool point, the model-implied probability that the point would be covered at a candidate threshold -- a control variate available because all candidate-label scores are computable without labels; (2) allocates label queries with probabilities proportional to the residual variance of the coverage indicator, i.e. to genuinely ambiguous points; (3) forms a Horvitz-Thompson debiased coverage estimate whose bias is zero regardless of proxy quality; and (4) selects the smallest threshold whose anytime-valid betting lower confidence bound on coverage exceeds 1-alpha, yielding prediction sets with exact finite-sample PAC (training-conditional) coverage under an adaptive, non-exchangeable design. We prove a label-complexity upper bound scaling with the ambiguity mass near the threshold and a matching lower bound showing no method can do better when model confidence is uninformative. Across ImageNet/CIFAR-100 classifiers, medical imaging, LLM multiple-choice QA, and CQR regression, ACTIVE-CAL matches the coverage and set size of random split conformal with 2-10x fewer labels, and we characterize when it does not.
problem_statement: Split conformal prediction spends hundreds to thousands of expensive ground-truth labels to estimate a single scalar quantile, and most of those labels are uninformative because the model is obviously right (or obviously wrong) on them. We hypothesize that (i) which calibration points get labeled matters enormously, (ii) by combining a model-derived proxy for the coverage indicator as a control variate with variance-optimal, adaptively chosen labeling probabilities and Horvitz-Thompson debiasing, one can certify 1-alpha coverage with 2-10x fewer labels than random-sample split conformal at the same set size, and (iii) this can be done with exact finite-sample (PAC / training-conditional) validity despite the labeling design being adaptive and non-exchangeable. We further hypothesize a matching lower bound: the achievable saving is governed by the 'ambiguity mass' of the score distribution near the calibration threshold, so label-efficient calibration is provably impossible exactly when the model's confidence is uninformative.

title: How Many Labels Does a Conformal Guarantee Cost? Active, Label-Efficient Calibration with Finite-Sample Validity

motivation_or_abstract: Conformal prediction is sold as a costless wrapper that turns any predictor into one with distribution-free coverage. We show it also turns any predictor into a leak. The wrapper's only learned parameter is a threshold equal to the ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))-th smallest conformity score of the calibration set: not an aggregate, but a single individual's score. We formalize a black-box threat model in which an adversary observes only prediction sets, and show that (a) the threshold can be recovered to arbitrary precision with O(log(1/eps)) queries by binary search along a continuous path in input space (e.g., interpolating between two images or perturbing a prompt), because set membership flips exactly when a score crosses the threshold; (b) once the threshold is known, testing whether a candidate record was in the calibration set reduces to comparing its score to the threshold, giving near-certain identification of the quantile record and, via a shadow-calibration likelihood-ratio test, materially elevated membership advantage for the rest of the calibration set; and (c) in adaptive conformal prediction the threshold is updated by other users' outcomes, so its trajectory leaks whether other users' predictions were covered, a cross-user side channel we exploit to reconstruct hidden labels. We prove that the empirical-quantile release has maximal individual sensitivity in rank space and derive attack-advantage bounds matching our measurements on CIFAR-100, ImageNet, Camelyon17 pathology, and LLM multiple-choice QA. Finally, we evaluate defenses -- rank randomization, subsample-and-aggregate thresholds, exponential-mechanism DP quantiles, and rate-limited/batched online updates -- and chart the resulting privacy-coverage-efficiency Pareto, finding that near-complete attack suppression often costs only a few percent in set size.
problem_statement: Split conformal prediction publishes, through every prediction set it emits, a threshold that is literally the conformity score of one individual calibration record (an order statistic), and in online/adaptive conformal prediction that threshold moves with other users' realized outcomes. We hypothesize that (i) an adversary with only black-box set-valued query access can extract the calibration quantile to near-machine precision, (ii) this yields membership inference against the calibration set that is substantially stronger than standard training-data MIA against the same model, especially for small calibration sets, and near-certain identification of the 'quantile individual', (iii) in adaptive conformal prediction the threshold trajectory leaks other users' labels/correctness, and (iv) rank-randomized and DP quantile defenses can suppress these attacks at a quantifiable, and surprisingly small, set-size cost.
